english: do unto others as you would have them do unto you
also: do as you would be done by

terms.latin: Ab aliō expectēs, alterī quod fēceris.
evidence: Sen. Ep. 94.43: ab aliō expectēs alterī quod fēceris
terms.comment: Literally “you may expect from another what you have done to another”: a line of Publilius Syrus, which Seneca quotes as a saying that needs no proof. It speaks of what comes back to you rather than of a duty, as the English does. Traupman spells it exspectēs.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, cited by printed page; each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections, checked against the editions named there.
Publilius is cited as the loci collection numbers him, by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library text.
